summary: Defines a YANG module called ietf-keystore for centrally configuring symmetric and asymmetric keys on a device. The secret values can be encrypted or hidden, and asymmetric keys can be tied to certificates. Like its companion truststore module, it can notify when certificates are close to expiring.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 9642 gives a network device one managed place to keep the cryptographic keys it needs for SSH, TLS and similar protocols. A management system can write the keys in, and read back which ones exist.

Each secret value can be given in the clear, marked as hidden when the device's own hardware holds it, or given encrypted along with a pointer to the key that did the encrypting. Keys can be linked to certificates, and the device raises a notification before a certificate expires.

subtitle: A YANG module for keeping a device's symmetric and asymmetric keys, and their certificates, in one place.

tldr.problem: Network devices need cryptographic keys for SSH, TLS and similar uses, and there was no common YANG way to configure them centrally, protect their secret values, or tie keys to certificates.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-keystore YANG module defines a keystore holding symmetric and asymmetric keys. Each secret can be stored in cleartext, hidden for hardware-protected keys, or encrypted by another key, and asymmetric keys can carry certificates. Groupings let other modules take a key inline or by reference.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one model for keys and certificates, with a notification when a certificate is about to expire and an action to generate a certificate signing request.

today: RFC 9642 was published in October 2024 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the crypto-types module in RFC 9640 and sits beside the truststore module in RFC 9641.

sections.title: What the Keystore Is For
sections.content:
This document presents a YANG 1.1 module called ietf-keystore that enables centralized configuration of both symmetric and asymmetric keys. The secret value of either kind of key may be encrypted or hidden, as described in the crypto-types module of RFC 9640, and asymmetric keys may be associated with certificates. Notifications are sent when certificates are about to expire.

The module defines many groupings intended for other modules to import. Among them are groupings that let a key be configured either inline, within the model that needs it, or as a reference to a key in the central keystore.

Servers with cryptographic hardware, such as a trusted platform module, get particular attention. The hardware hides the secret key values, and it is commonly initialised in the factory with a built-in asymmetric key whose public half is carried in an identity certificate, such as an Initial Device Identifier certificate.

The RFC is part of a collection that together supports configuring both the clients and servers of NETCONF and RESTCONF. The crypto-types module has no dependencies of its own, and both the truststore module and this keystore module depend on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The module gives a device one place to keep its cryptographic keys, configured from a management system rather than typed in by hand. It also gives other modules a way to say "use this key" without repeating the key itself.

sections.title: The Shape of the Keystore
sections.content:
The module defines four features: central-keystore-supported, inline-definitions-supported, asymmetric-keys and symmetric-keys. It defines two typedefs, central-symmetric-key-ref and central-asymmetric-key-ref, both of them leaf references used to point at a key held in the central keystore.

The protocol-accessible node is a single container, keystore, which exists only when the central-keystore-supported feature is on. It expands to the keystore grouping, which holds two lists. asymmetric-keys holds asymmetric-key entries keyed by name. Each has a public key format and a public key, and a private key given in one of three ways: as cleartext binary data, as a hidden key where the leaf is empty and the hardware keeps the value, or as an encrypted value with a reference to the key that did the encrypting and the format of that encrypted value. An asymmetric key can also carry a list of certificates, each with a name and the certificate data, and each certificate can raise a notification giving its expiry date.

The symmetric-keys list holds symmetric-key entries keyed by name, each with a key format and the value in the same three forms.

The module also defines a generate-csr action on an asymmetric key. Its input gives the request format and the information to use, and its output is a PKCS #10 certificate signing request.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one container with two lists, one for asymmetric keys and one for symmetric keys. Each key has a name, and its secret value can be given in the clear, marked as hidden when the hardware holds it, or given encrypted along with a pointer to the key that encrypted it.

sections.title: Groupings for Other Modules
sections.content:
The module defines seven groupings. The encrypted-by-grouping defines a choice between referencing a symmetric key in the central keystore and referencing an asymmetric one. The central-asymmetric-key-certificate-ref-grouping defines a reference to a certificate in two parts: the name of the asymmetric key the certificate is associated with, and the name of the certificate itself.

Four groupings offer a choice between defining a key inline and referring to the central keystore: the symmetric key grouping, the asymmetric key grouping, the asymmetric key with certificates grouping, and the end-entity certificate with key grouping. Each is a choice statement whose cases are gated by feature statements, so a consuming module can offer the inline option, the central keystore option, or both. Additional cases may be augmented in for a module that keeps its keys somewhere else.

The keystore-grouping is the whole keystore structure, kept separate from the protocol-accessible nodes so that other modules can instantiate a keystore in a different location if they need to. The RFC calls the top-level instance the central keystore; every other instance is not central.
sections.plainLanguage: Other modules import groupings from this one. The important ones let a module say "either give the key here, or point at one in the central keystore", and let it refer to a certificate by naming both its key and the certificate.

sections.title: Built-In Keys
sections.content:
Some servers support keys built into them. Built-in keys MAY be set during the manufacturing process, or generated the first time the server boots or a particular service such as SSH is enabled. They are hidden keys expected to be set by a vendor-specific process, and any ability for operators to set or modify them is outside the scope of this document.

The defining characteristic is that built-in keys are provided by the server rather than configured, so they are present in the operational datastore, and in the system datastore if that is implemented.

The RFC shows what a server in its factory default state looks like. The built-in key is an asymmetric key with a hidden private key and one certificate, the manufacturer-generated IDevID certificate, and the origin annotation says it came from the system. It then shows what happens after a deployment-specific certificate is added: the operational datastore still reports the built-in key with the origin of the system, and the new certificate is listed with the origin of the intended configuration. The hidden private key is never exposed in either case.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices come with a key from the factory, and its secret half never leaves the hardware. The model reports such a key as part of the device's current state rather than as configuration, and marks it as coming from the system rather than from the operator.

sections.title: Encrypting Keys in Configuration
sections.content:
Section 4 describes an approach that lets the symmetric and asymmetric keys on a server be encrypted, so that a backup and restore does not expose raw key data in transit. The section is not normative; it answers how a configuration whose secrets are encrypted by a built-in key can be backed up from one server and restored on another when each server has its own primary key.

The ability to encrypt configured keys depends on a key encryption key, which may be symmetric or asymmetric. If it is symmetric, the server MUST provide an API so that administrators can encrypt other keys without knowing its value. If it is asymmetric, the server SHOULD provide such an API, or assume that administrators can encrypt using the public half. In either case the server must be able to reach the key encryption key at run time so that it can decrypt the other keys.

Each time a new key is configured it SHOULD be encrypted by a key encryption key. Implementations SHOULD provide an API that generates a key and encrypts it at the same time, so that the cleartext value never becomes known to the administrators. The encrypted key is then configured through the encrypted-symmetric-key or encrypted-private-key nodes, which hold both the encrypted value and a reference to the key that encrypted it.

Migrating a configuration to another server is only possible if that server has the same key encryption key. To decouple the crypto officer from the ordinary administrators, the RFC introduces a special key encryption key called the primary key, commonly a globally unique built-in asymmetric key whose private half is hidden and whose public half sits in an identity certificate. The primary key encrypts a shared key encryption key, and that one encrypts the keys the administrators configure. A crypto officer can then encrypt the same shared key offline for many servers and hand the results to ordinary administrators. To migrate, the administrator replaces one entry, the encrypted shared key, and the rest of the configuration comes across intact.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can encrypt the keys it is given, so that a backup does not carry readable secrets. The key that does the encrypting has to be present on the target device too. The RFC arranges this with two layers: a built-in key that only the manufacturer has, and a shared key that the manufacturer's officer encrypts once for every device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The keystore exists to protect its contents from unauthorised disclosure and modification. It is RECOMMENDED that server implementations encrypt the keystore contents when writing them to non-volatile memory, and zeroize the contents that were decrypted in volatile memory when they are no longer in use. The contents may be encrypted individually, using the encrypted value formats, or by encryption at the persistence layer. If cleartext values are stored, which is not recommended, persistence-layer encryption SHOULD be used. If the contents are not encrypted when persisted, the server MUST ensure the persisted storage is inaccessible.

The module enables the configuration of private keys without constraining what a key may be used for, such as signing, decryption or both. It also does not constrain the use of the associated public keys except in the context of a configured certificate, where the certificate does constrain it.

Access is over NETCONF or RESTCONF, which have mandatory secure transport layers and mandatory mutual authentication, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model is the way to restrict what each user may reach. The RFC warns that this module uses groupings from other modules that may define sensitive nodes, so the security considerations of those modules apply. Read access to the readable data nodes should be controlled, because some of them may be sensitive in some environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Secrets should be encrypted when the device stores them and should be wiped from memory once used. Access to the keystore has to be restricted, because reading it gives away key material.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA has registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-keystore in the "ns" subregistry of the "IETF XML Registry", and the module name ietf-keystore in the "YANG Module Names" subregistry of the "YANG Parameters" registry. The module's prefix is ks and its revision date is 2024-10-10.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers the module's name and its XML namespace, which is what tells a management system which vocabulary it is looking at.
